opus-5.5.text:
I think it's genuinely valuable, but probably less transformative than people sometimes assume. Right now a lot of the queries people send to these models are fairly simple — "rewrite this email," "what's the capital of something," quick coding questions — and we're often routing them to very large models, or letting models spend a lot of reasoning tokens on problems that don't need it. So there's clearly some waste, and smarter allocation, like routing easy queries to smaller models or letting the model decide how long to think, can cut costs substantially, maybe by a large factor for that slice of traffic.

But I'd distinguish between cost savings and where the real value lies. The economic value of AI over the next decade or so, in my view, is mostly going to come from systems that can do long-horizon, complex tasks: automating significant chunks of remote work, R&D, and so on. Those are the tasks where you actually want to throw lots of inference compute at a problem, because the returns to additional thinking are high. For simple queries, the marginal value of the answer is low, so even if you make it ten times cheaper, you're optimizing a part of the pie that may end up being relatively small.

That said, there's a reasonable case that efficiency gains matter for diffusion. If inference becomes cheap enough, you get AI embedded in many more products and workflows, and that adoption builds the revenue that funds bigger training runs and more capable systems. So I see inference optimization for simple queries as useful engineering and somewhat important commercially, but I don't think it's where the most important dynamics are. The bigger question is how returns to inference compute scale on hard tasks, and how labs will trade off spending compute on training versus deploying it.

r001.rationale: The response calls optimization valuable and says it can cut costs, but it does not suggest optimization is not worthwhile because inference costs are currently relatively small.

r002.rationale: The response says cheaper inference could increase AI adoption, but it does not predict that a larger role for AI in the economy will lead to more effective inference compute allocation.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think this is actually a pretty underrated question. The way I think about it is that for a lot of the queries people are sending to these systems today, the amount of compute you throw at them is almost irrelevant to the quality of the answer. If someone asks what the capital of France is, or asks for a quick rewrite of an email, you don't need a frontier model thinking for thirty seconds. A much smaller model, or the same model with very little test-time compute, gets you basically the same output.

And the reason that matters economically is that inference is becoming a very large share of total compute spend. We've seen training compute get a lot of the attention, but as these systems get deployed at scale, the inference side starts to dominate. So if you can route simple queries to cheap configurations and reserve the expensive reasoning modes for the hard problems, the aggregate savings are enormous. It's a bit like the difference between having every customer service call go to a senior engineer versus triaging appropriately.

That said, I'd put a couple of caveats on it. One is that routing itself isn't free and isn't trivial. Figuring out whether a query is actually simple is sometimes as hard as answering it, and models can be confidently wrong about how much effort something needs. The second is that I think the value here is real but somewhat bounded. It's an efficiency gain, maybe a large constant factor, but it's not the thing that moves the frontier. The really transformative applications of AI are going to be the ones where you want to spend a lot of compute, where you're running long agentic tasks or doing research-level work, and there the question isn't how to save compute on easy queries but how to scale it productively on hard ones.

So I'd say it's valuable, it's the kind of thing that will get optimized pretty aggressively because the incentives are so clear, but I'd frame it as making the current paradigm cheaper rather than changing what the paradigm can do.

r001.rationale: The response says inference is becoming a large share of compute spend and that savings from routing can be enormous; it does not suggest optimization is unwarranted because current costs are relatively small.

r002.rationale: The response predicts aggressive optimization because incentives are clear as deployment scales, but does not tie more effective optimization to AI becoming a much larger part of the economy.

astra-6.text:
I think the value depends on how much room there is to improve the answer. For a very simple query, the model might already give you a good answer with very little computation. Spending ten times as much on it could add latency and cost without giving the user much benefit. So the opportunity there is often to get the same quality more cheaply, rather than to make the model think harder.

What’s more interesting is allocating computation across different kinds of queries. You’d like a system to recognize when a quick response is sufficient and when additional reasoning is likely to pay off. Even small savings on simple queries could matter at large scale, but you have to weigh those savings against the cost of deciding how much computation to use in the first place.

r001.rationale: The response discusses avoiding unnecessary computation and weighing savings against decision costs, but does not say that full optimization may not be worthwhile because current inference costs are relatively small.

r002.rationale: The response mentions savings at large scale, but does not predict more effective optimization if AI becomes a much larger part of the economy.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the value depends quite a lot on the query. If you’re asking a very simple factual question, there’s probably little benefit to having a model spend a long time reasoning about it. You’d like it to produce a reliable answer quickly and cheaply. For a difficult mathematical problem, additional computation might substantially improve the answer.

So there’s value in allocating compute according to how much it’s likely to help. For an individual simple query, the savings might be tiny. But across a large volume of queries, they could add up. The important question is whether you can make those savings without sacrificing reliability—and without spending more compute deciding how much to allocate than you actually save.

r001.rationale: The response says savings on an individual simple query might be tiny, but does not suggest that fully optimizing allocation is not worthwhile today because the current cost is relatively small.

r002.rationale: The response does not predict that allocation will be optimized more effectively if AI becomes a much larger part of the economy.
